title: The Banality of Being Wrong: Truth-Telling vs. Trolling
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos defends her habit of asking literacy professors to cite the research behind their claims after a commenter accused her of trolling, epistemic trespassing and the Dunning-Kruger effect. She draws on Sunita Sah on defiance, Noah Smith's two-paper test for a 'mud moat' of literature, Kirschner and Neelen on eminence-based education and Hewitt and Sachdeva on questions teachers should ask of PD. Her central claim is that being wrong is banal and forgivable, but failing to act on evidence, whether a professor refusing to engage or a district keeping flawed benchmark books, is the real harm when children's reading futures are at stake. She concludes that the cost of compliance has to be weighed against the cost of defiance.
points: Asking an expert to support a claim with research is not disrespect, and credentials do not exempt public claims from scrutiny.
Noah Smith's test of asking for just two exemplar papers is offered as a defence against being flooded with a vast literature that may be a mud moat.
Education is portrayed as still steeped in eminence-based rather than evidence-based decision making, so teachers need to be equipped to evaluate research.
The danger is not being wrong but clinging to unsupported methods or keeping the status quo, as in the district assessment director's refusal to change benchmark books.
Distance between decision-makers and classrooms, as Sowell notes, makes it easy to pay no price for being wrong.
quotes: Dr. Johnson is a public figure publishing books and a Substack as well as making videos, so as far as I’m concerned, his claims are fair game. Each and every assertion he makes is subject to strict scrutiny if he wishes to be taken seriously.

I certainly don’t view underlings at my school like that. I want teachers who lack my reading specialist credential to challenge me based on both their experience and expertise as evidenced by their time in the classroom as well as their knowledge of best practices.

My concern is not with being wrong but with a failure to do something about being wrong and, in some cases, displaying a cavalier attitude about clinging to unsupported methods and then taking umbrage when challenged about those methods. I am especially troubled by an oh, well attitude by some when presented with what is at stake. This is the banality I am referring to: a bored bow to business as usual.
Teachers shouldn’t have to take research claims on faith. Like physicians reading medical journals, educators should be equipped to read, interpret, and evaluate research findings.

My question: Since when is asking someone to support their claims a sign of disrespect? If we’re dealing with fragile egos as we attempt to have frank discussions, then we are in the wrong field of work. We can’t walk on eggshells or soften our speech or our stance because our stomping ground offends the sensibilities of others. Our job is getting reading right, not showing deference to authority and a blind trust of the status quo.
She listened attentively and asked all the right questions. And yet, at the end of the meeting, she walked away asserting that they would retain the status quo.
